claims.source: Such a system might lead not only to the loss of endogenous organics, but also to the influx of subsurface microorganisms that could complicate the detection of any surviving organics, as well as potentially metabolizing them.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the open system nature of fossil bone.

claims.claim: The possibility of a microbiome inhabiting fossil bone is very high.
claims.source: The possibility of a microbiome inhabiting fossil bone is very high, especially given that decades of research have revealed the existence of a substantial 'deep biosphere' of living microorganisms actively degrading everything organic from shallow soil organic matter to deeply buried petroleum (Onstott, 2016; Magnabosco et al., 2018), even in million year old permafrost (Amato et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on the deep biosphere.

claims.claim: Decades of research have revealed the existence of a substantial 'deep biosphere' of living microorganisms.
claims.source: The possibility of a microbiome inhabiting fossil bone is very high, especially given that decades of research have revealed the existence of a substantial 'deep biosphere' of living microorganisms actively degrading everything organic from shallow soil organic matter to deeply buried petroleum (Onstott, 2016; Magnabosco et al., 2018), even in million year old permafrost (Amato et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Onstott, 2016 and Magnabosco et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Living microorganisms have been found in million year old permafrost.
claims.source: The possibility of a microbiome inhabiting fossil bone is very high, especially given that decades of research have revealed the existence of a substantial 'deep biosphere' of living microorganisms actively degrading everything organic from shallow soil organic matter to deeply buried petroleum (Onstott, 2016; Magnabosco et al., 2018), even in million year old permafrost (Amato et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Amato et al., 2010.

claims.claim: The null hypothesis is that complex biomolecules recovered from dinosaur bones are not original material, more likely representing recent contamination.
claims.source: Since there are theoretical and empirical reasons to believe that dinosaur organics are unlikely to persist for tens of millions of years, and given the potential for contamination, we argue that the null hypothesis is that complex biomolecules (e.g. nucleic acids or proteins) recovered from dinosaur bones are not original material, more likely representing recent contamination.
claims.evidence: This is the authors' proposed null hypothesis based on theoretical and empirical considerations.

claims.claim: Organic material recovered from fossil dinosaur bone will differ in composition from modern vertebrate proteins and tissues, beyond differences expected through normal diagenesis.
claims.source: This hypothesis makes a series of testable predictions: (1) organic material recovered from fossil dinosaur bone will differ in composition (both chemistry and structure) from modern vertebrate proteins and tissues, beyond differences expected through normal diagenesis
claims.evidence: This is a testable prediction derived from the null hypothesis.

claims.claim: Fossils will show evidence for microbial presence.
claims.source: (2) fossils will show evidence for microbial presence (e.g., through nucleic acids or protein)
claims.evidence: This is a testable prediction derived from the null hypothesis.

claims.claim: Fossil bone organic material will show signatures of recent biological activity.
claims.source: (3) fossil bone organic material will show signatures of recent biological activity (e.g. L-amino acid dominance or 14C abundance, which would suggest that the fossils are not isolated from surface processes).
claims.evidence: This is a testable prediction derived from the null hypothesis.

claims.claim: Samples of Late Cretaceous fossil dinosaur bone were obtained from the Dinosaur Park Formation (Late Campanian) in Dinosaur Provincial Park, Alberta, Canada.
claims.source: Samples of Late Cretaceous fossil dinosaur bone, along with associated sediment and soil controls were obtained from the Dinosaur Park Formation (Late Campanian) in Dinosaur Provincial Park, Alberta, Canada (Appendix 1—figures 8–20, Appendix 1—table 2).
claims.evidence: This describes the source of the samples used in the study.

claims.claim: The Dinosaur Park Formation is a well-sampled, alluvial-paralic unit deposited during a transgressive phase of the Western Interior Seaway.
claims.source: The Dinosaur Park Formation is a well-sampled, alluvial-paralic unit deposited during a transgressive phase of the Western Interior Seaway.
claims.evidence: This is geological information about the formation.

claims.claim: A diverse vertebrate fauna has been documented from the Dinosaur Park Formation by more than a century of collection.
claims.source: A diverse vertebrate fauna has been documented from the formation by more than a century of collection (Currie and Koppelhus, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Currie and Koppelhus, 2005.

claims.claim: The bone samples were collected from a monodominant bonebed (BB180) of the centrosaurine Centrosaurus apertus.
claims.source: The bone samples were collected from a monodominant bonebed (BB180) of the centrosaurine Centrosaurus apertus (Ornithischia; Ceratopsidae), located 3 m above the contact with the underlying Oldman Formation (precise location data available at the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology).
claims.evidence: This describes the specific source of the bone samples.

claims.claim: The bonebed is located 3 m above the contact with the underlying Oldman Formation.
claims.source: The bone samples were collected from a monodominant bonebed (BB180) of the centrosaurine Centrosaurus apertus (Ornithischia; Ceratopsidae), located 3 m above the contact with the underlying Oldman Formation (precise location data available at the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology).
claims.evidence: This is stratigraphic information about the sample location.

claims.claim: The mudstone-hosted bone-bearing horizon is an aggregation of disarticulated but densely packed bones, with a vertical relief of 15–20 cm.
claims.source: The mudstone-hosted bone-bearing horizon is an aggregation of disarticulated but densely packed bones, with a vertical relief of 15–20 cm.
claims.evidence: This describes the taphonomic characteristics of the bonebed.

claims.claim: The recovered skeletal remains are nearly exclusively from Ceratopsidae, with all diagnostic ceratopsid material assignable to Centrosaurus apertus.
claims.source: Similar to other ceratopsid bonebeds from the same stratigraphic interval (Ryan et al., 2001; Eberth and Getty, 2005), the recovered skeletal remains are nearly exclusively from Ceratopsidae, and with all diagnostic ceratopsid material assignable to Centrosaurus apertus, with the site interpreted as a mass-death assemblage.
claims.evidence: This describes the taxonomic composition of the bonebed.

claims.claim: The site is interpreted as a mass-death assemblage.
claims.source: Similar to other ceratopsid bonebeds from the same stratigraphic interval (Ryan et al., 2001; Eberth and Getty, 2005), the recovered skeletal remains are nearly exclusively from Ceratopsidae, and with all diagnostic ceratopsid material assignable to Centrosaurus apertus, with the site interpreted as a mass-death assemblage.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the taphonomic origin of the bonebed.

claims.claim: Aseptic techniques were implemented during excavation to minimize contamination.
claims.source: At this point, aseptic techniques were then implemented to expose more of the bone in order to determine its size and orientation.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology used during sample collection.

claims.claim: It is practically impossible to excavate fossils in a truly sterile manner.
claims.source: It is necessary to qualify the usage of the term 'aseptic' in this study. Paleontological field techniques have changed little over the last century, and it is practically impossible to excavate fossils in a truly sterile manner (e.g. the process of matrix removal induces exposure, the wind can carry environmental contaminants onto exposed fossils, etc.).
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of field methodology.

claims.claim: Centrosaurus bone vessels were white, Si-dominated with O present, contained holes, and were sometimes infilled with a slightly more prominent C peak internally.
claims.source: VPSEM and EDS of HCl demineralized, freeze-dried dinosaur bones revealed that vessels (and rare fibrous fragments) (Figure 1A,D–E,H–J) were white, Si-dominated with O present, contained holes, and were sometimes infilled with a slightly more prominent C peak internally.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from VPSEM and EDS analysis, with reference to Figure 1.

claims.claim: Vessels in Centrosaurus bone occurred alongside white quartz crystals and smaller reddish minerals with high-Si content and Ba present.
claims.source: Vessels occurred alongside white quartz crystals, which had strong Si peaks and overall were elementally similar to the vessels, and smaller reddish minerals, originally presumed to be iron oxide or pyrite, but which had high-Si content with Ba also present.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from VPSEM and EDS analysis.

claims.claim: Demineralization products of chicken bone and Pleistocene-Holocene shark tooth were much more homogenous and consisted of large fibrous masses.
claims.source: Demineralization products differed from those of chicken bone (Figure 1C,G,M) and Pleistocene-Holocene shark tooth (Figure 1B,F,L), which were much more homogenous and consisted of large fibrous masses.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative finding from microscopy, with reference to Figure 1.

claims.claim: Chicken bone and shark tooth demineralization products were enriched in C, O, N, and S.
claims.source: These more recent samples were enriched in C, O, N, and S, but the shark tooth also had a strong Fe signature and a relatively more prominent S peak than the chicken bone.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from EDS analysis.

claims.claim: The shark tooth had a strong Fe signature and a relatively more prominent S peak than the chicken bone.
claims.source: These more recent samples were enriched in C, O, N, and S, but the shark tooth also had a strong Fe signature and a relatively more prominent S peak than the chicken bone.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from EDS analysis.

claims.claim: The chicken demineralisation product was white, while that of the shark tooth was black.
claims.source: The chicken demineralisation product was white, while that of the shark tooth was black.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from visual inspection.

claims.claim: The dinosaur bone yielded different structures when the bone apatite was removed compared to the more recent bone.
claims.source: These results show that the dinosaur bone yielded different structures when the bone apatite was removed compared to the more recent bone (i.e. primarily vessels as opposed to large fibrous masses).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the microscopy results.

claims.claim: The dinosaur vessels are relatively inorganic in composition compared to the more recent bone, consistent with a mineralized biofilm.
claims.source: Furthermore, the dinosaur vessels are relatively inorganic in composition compared to the more recent bone, consistent with a mineralized biofilm (Schultze-Lam et al., 1996; Decho, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the EDS results, supported by citations.

claims.claim: ATR FTIR of a HCl demineralized vessel from subterranean Centrosaurus bone revealed somewhat poorly resolved, broad organic peaks.
claims.source: ATR FTIR of a HCl demineralized, freeze-dried vessel from subterranean Centrosaurus bone revealed somewhat poorly resolved, broad organic peaks (Figure 2C) that were close in position to peaks that might be expected from various CH, CO, and amide bonds, as well as water, phosphate, and potentially carbonate and silicate bonds (Lindgren et al., 2011; Surmik et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017); also see publicly available NIST libraries).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from ATR FTIR analysis, with reference to Figure 2.

claims.claim: The ATR FTIR peaks in the dinosaur bone demineralization products could be consistent with various organic bonds present in more recent bone demineralization products.
claims.source: These results show how, although potentially poorly resolved, the ATR FTIR peaks in the dinosaur bone demineralization products could be consistent with various organic bonds present in more recent bone demineralization products.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the ATR FTIR results.

claims.claim: The organic bonds detected by ATR FTIR are not necessarily ancient, endogenous, or protein-derived.
claims.source: However, note that these bonds are relatively simple and could therefore be present in various organic molecules. Furthermore, they are not necessarily ancient, endogenous, or protein-derived.
claims.evidence: This is a cautionary interpretation of the ATR FTIR results.

claims.claim: Centrosaurus bone had a low pyrolysate yield as evidenced by significant column bleed at the end of the run.
claims.source: Centrosaurus bone had a low pyrolysate yield (Figure 3B) as evidenced by the significant column bleed at the end of the run and contained mostly early eluting compounds.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from Py-GC-MS analysis, with reference to Figure 3.

claims.claim: The pyrogram for Centrosaurus bone does not match that of modern collagen-containing bone.
claims.source: The pyrogram for Centrosaurus bone does not match that of modern collagen-containing bone (Figure 3A), which contained many clear protein pyrolysis products such as nitriles and amides, and was most similar to mudstone matrix (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative finding from Py-GC-MS analysis, with reference to Figure 3.

claims.claim: The pyrogram for Centrosaurus bone was most similar to mudstone matrix.
claims.source: The pyrogram for Centrosaurus bone does not match that of modern collagen-containing bone (Figure 3A), which contained many clear protein pyrolysis products such as nitriles and amides, and was most similar to mudstone matrix (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative finding from Py-GC-MS analysis, with reference to Figure 3.

claims.claim: Subterranean Centrosaurus bone pyrolysates included alkylated benzenes and some polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.
claims.source: Subterranean Centrosaurus bone pyrolysates included alkylated benzenes and some polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (e.g. naphthalenes and fluorenes), and these can also be detected in the surrounding mudstone matrix (Figure 3C) and humic acid standard (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from Py-GC-MS analysis, with reference to Figure 3.

claims.claim: Weak n-alkane/n-alkene doublets were possibly detected in the Late Cretaceous bones.
claims.source: Weak n-alkane/n-alkene doublets were possibly detected in the Late Cretaceous bones (Figure 4A–D), and such doublets were also observed in the surrounding mudstone matrix (Figure 3C) and humic acid standard (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from Py-GC-MS analysis, with reference to Figures 3 and 4.

claims.claim: The dinosaur bone lacked any clear pyrolysis products indicative of high levels of protein preservation.
claims.source: These results show how the dinosaur bone lacked any clear pyrolysis products indicative of high levels of protein preservation and instead had a chemical composition that more closely resembles potential environmental sources (i.e. mudstone matrix or humic acids) than bone proteins.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the Py-GC-MS results.

claims.claim: The dinosaur bone had a chemical composition that more closely resembles potential environmental sources than bone proteins.
claims.source: These results show how the dinosaur bone lacked any clear pyrolysis products indicative of high levels of protein preservation and instead had a chemical composition that more closely resembles potential environmental sources (i.e. mudstone matrix or humic acids) than bone proteins.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the Py-GC-MS results.

claims.claim: Homologous series of n-alkane/n-alkene doublets may signify the presence of a kerogen-like substance in the dinosaur bone.
claims.source: Homologous series of n-alkane/n-alkene doublets may signify the presence of a kerogen-like substance which could potentially be an ancient lipid-derived geopolymer in the dinosaur bone.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the Py-GC-MS results.

claims.claim: Matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone had a total hydrolysable amino acid compositional profile that did not match collagen.
claims.source: Matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone had a total hydrolysable amino acid (THAA) compositional profile that did not match collagen (Figure 6A,F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figure 6.

claims.claim: Matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone appeared to be dominated by Gly, with Tyr also prominent, while being highly depleted in all the other amino acids.
claims.source: The matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone appeared to be dominated by Gly, with Tyr also prominent, while being highly depleted in all the other amino acids.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from HPLC amino acid analysis.

claims.claim: Surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bone showed a different THAA composition to the matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone.
claims.source: Surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bone from the same outcrop showed a different THAA composition to the matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone, even when examining bone eroded out of the BB180 quarry itself (Figure 6B,F).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figure 6.

claims.claim: The uncovered subterranean Centrosaurus bone did not match the matrix-surrounded subterranean bone and was similar to the surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bone in THAA composition.
claims.source: Furthermore, the uncovered subterranean Centrosaurus bone did not match the matrix-surrounded subterranean bone and was similar to the surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bone in THAA composition.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative finding from HPLC amino acid analysis.

claims.claim: Exposure to the surface changes the amino acid profile within Cretaceous fossils.
claims.source: These results suggest that not only did the subterranean dinosaur bone not have an amino acid composition similar to collagen (i.e. Gallus and reference bone), but also that exposure to the surface changes the amino acid profile within these Cretaceous fossils.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the HPLC amino acid analysis results.

claims.claim: Subterranean Centrosaurus bone had a far lower THAA concentration than modern chicken bone.
claims.source: Subterranean Centrosaurus bone had a far lower THAA concentration (summed total of all amino acids measured) than did the modern chicken bone (Figure 7A), as would be expected, and the uncovered subterranean Centrosaurus bone showed a higher THAA concentration than the matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figure 7.

claims.claim: The uncovered subterranean Centrosaurus bone showed a higher THAA concentration than the matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone.
claims.source: Subterranean Centrosaurus bone had a far lower THAA concentration (summed total of all amino acids measured) than did the modern chicken bone (Figure 7A), as would be expected, and the uncovered subterranean Centrosaurus bone showed a higher THAA concentration than the matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figure 7.

claims.claim: Late Cretaceous bone tended to be L-amino acid dominated when amino acids were above detection limit.
claims.source: Late Cretaceous bone tended to be L-amino acid dominated when amino acids were above detection limit (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from amino acid racemization analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claims.claim: Low levels of racemization suggest that the amino acids in the dinosaur bone are not particularly ancient.
claims.source: These low levels of racemization suggest that the amino acids in the dinosaur bone are not particularly ancient.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the racemization data.

claims.claim: The adjacent mudstone matrix did not match the subterranean Centrosaurus bone in THAA compositional profile.
claims.source: The adjacent mudstone matrix did not match the subterranean Centrosaurus bone in THAA compositional profile (Figure 6D,F).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figure 6.

claims.claim: Surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bone showed some degree of similarity to topsoil in THAA composition.
claims.source: Surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bone showed some degree of similarity to topsoil in THAA composition (Figure 6E,F), as did the various mudstone samples.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figure 6.

claims.claim: Matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone showed the most different THAA compositional profile within the study.
claims.source: Matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone showed the most different THAA compositional profile within the study (i.e. greatest separation from other data points in PC space).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the PCA results.

claims.claim: The greatest variation between the samples was in relative Gly and Tyr concentrations.
claims.source: The greatest variation between the samples of this study was in relative Gly and Tyr concentrations, with the matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone tending to have notably higher Gly and Tyr than collagen.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from HPLC amino acid analysis.

claims.claim: Subterranean dinosaur bone had a different amino acid composition than the surrounding mudstone.
claims.source: These results suggest that subterranean dinosaur bone had a different amino acid composition than the surrounding mudstone and that the amino acid composition changes upon surface exposure, approaching that of topsoil.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the HPLC amino acid analysis results.

claims.claim: The amino acid composition of dinosaur bone changes upon surface exposure, approaching that of topsoil.
claims.source: These results suggest that subterranean dinosaur bone had a different amino acid composition than the surrounding mudstone and that the amino acid composition changes upon surface exposure, approaching that of topsoil.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the HPLC amino acid analysis results.

claims.claim: Topsoil showed a greater THAA concentration than subterranean and surface-eroded Centrosaurus bones, but not as high as modern chicken bones.
claims.source: Topsoil showed a greater THAA concentration than subterranean and surface-eroded Centrosaurus bones, but not as high as modern chicken bones (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figure 7.

claims.claim: Mudstone tended to have a very low THAA concentration, even compared to some of the Late Cretaceous bone samples.
claims.source: Mudstone tended to have a very low THAA concentration, even compared to some of the Late Cretaceous bone samples (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figure 7.

claims.claim: Topsoil contained a high amino acid concentration with relatively high rates of protein degradation, indicative of active biological accumulation and recycling.
claims.source: These results show that topsoil contained a high amino acid concentration with relatively high rates of protein degradation, indicative of active biological accumulation and recycling, while mudstone contained low concentrations with very recent amino acids, indicative of low residence times of proteins within the mudstone.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid concentration and racemization data.

claims.claim: Mudstone contained low amino acid concentrations with very recent amino acids, indicative of low residence times of proteins within the mudstone.
claims.source: These results show that topsoil contained a high amino acid concentration with relatively high rates of protein degradation, indicative of active biological accumulation and recycling, while mudstone contained low concentrations with very recent amino acids, indicative of low residence times of proteins within the mudstone.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid concentration and racemization data.

claims.claim: Fossil bones appeared to show instances of relatively greater accumulation of amino acids than the mudstone but with very recent amino acids.
claims.source: The fossil bones appeared to show instances of relatively greater accumulation of amino acids than the mudstone but with very recent amino acids, indicative of preferential localization of biologically active amino acids to the bone compared to the mudstone, but with less amino acid content than topsoil.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid concentration and racemization data.

claims.claim: Pleistocene-Holocene surface-eroded shark teeth had THAA compositional profiles that closely matched collagen.
claims.source: Pleistocene-Holocene surface-eroded shark teeth had THAA compositional profiles that closely matched collagen (Figure 6A,C,F) and fairly high amino acid concentration with THAA concentrations between those of subterranean Centrosaurus bone and modern chicken bone (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figures 6 and 7.

claims.claim: Pleistocene-Holocene surface-eroded shark teeth had consistently high racemization, even more so than the topsoil sample.
claims.source: Pleistocene-Holocene surface-eroded shark teeth, unlike the Late Cretaceous bone and mudstone, had consistently high racemization (Table 1), even more so than the topsoil sample.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from amino acid racemization analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claims.claim: The Pleistocene-Holocene teeth contained detectable, ancient amino acids consistent with endogenous collagen.
claims.source: These results suggest that the Pleistocene-Holocene teeth contained detectable, ancient amino acids consistent with endogenous collagen.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid analysis results.

claims.claim: Total organic carbon content was higher in the subterranean and surface-eroded Centrosaurus bone than the matrix.
claims.source: Total organic carbon (TOC) content was higher in the subterranean and surface-eroded Centrosaurus bone than the matrix, even the directly adjacent matrix, and was comparable to that found in the topsoil (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from radiocarbon AMS analysis, with reference to Table 2.

claims.claim: The organic carbon content in the Centrosaurus bones was significantly lower than the 82–71 ka Yarnton bovine bone sample known to contain well-preserved collagen.
claims.source: However, the organic carbon content in the Centrosaurus bones was significantly lower than the 82–71 ka Yarnton bovine bone sample known to contain well-preserved (radiocarbon-dead) collagen (Cook et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative finding from radiocarbon AMS analysis, with citation.

claims.claim: TOC in the Centrosaurus bone was not found to be radiocarbon dead.
claims.source: TOC in the Centrosaurus bone was not found to be radiocarbon dead, but did exhibit lower F14C values than both the mudstone and especially the topsoil.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from radiocarbon AMS analysis.

claims.claim: Approximately 26% of the C in subterranean Centrosaurus bone originates in the adjacent mudstone matrix, based on a simple two-end-member mixing model.
claims.source: Assuming all endogenous bone C is radiocarbon 'dead', based on these F14C values, a simple two-end-member mixing model would suggest that ~26% of the C in subterranean Centrosaurus bone originates in the adjacent mudstone matrix (for formula, see Appendix 1 under the section entitled Carbon analysis).
claims.evidence: This is a calculation based on radiocarbon data.

claims.claim: The fossil dinosaur bone yielded a TOC content similar to relatively rich environmental carbon sources, such as topsoil.
claims.source: The fossil dinosaur bone therefore yielded a TOC content similar to relatively rich environmental carbon sources, such as topsoil, but not as high as more recent bone proteins.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the radiocarbon data.

claims.claim: Some of the C in the fossil dinosaur bone is potentially ancient, but there is still a sizable contribution of recent C from the immediate environment.
claims.source: Although, some of the C in the fossil dinosaur bone is potentially ancient, there is still a sizable contribution of recent C from the immediate environment, consistent with the presence of a microbiome.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the radiocarbon data.

claims.claim: DNA concentration was about 50 times higher in subterranean Centrosaurus bone than in adjacent mudstone matrix.
claims.source: DNA concentration was about 50 times higher in subterranean Centrosaurus bone than in adjacent mudstone matrix (Table 3; Appendix 1—table 25).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from DNA extraction and quantification, with reference to Table 3.

claims.claim: PI staining for DNA on EDTA demineralized Centrosaurus bone revealed multi-cell aggregates forming organic vessel and fibrous conglomerate structures that fluoresce red.
claims.source: PI staining for DNA on EDTA demineralized Centrosaurus bone revealed multi-cell aggregates forming organic vessel and fibrous conglomerate structures that fluoresce red (Figure 8A–D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from fluorescence microscopy, with reference to Figure 8.

claims.claim: The DNA concentration in the bone indicates a cell concentration of ~4×10^8 cells/g.
claims.source: The DNA concentration in the bone indicates a cell concentration of ~4×108 cells/g (calculation of cell abundance from DNA based on that of Magnabosco et al., 2018; also see Appendix 1—table 26).
claims.evidence: This is a calculation based on DNA concentration data.

claims.claim: The observed THAA concentration indicates ~3×10^8 cells/g in the bone.
claims.source: This is fairly similar to the observed THAA concentration indicating ~3×108 cells/g (calculation of cell abundance from total amino acids based on that of Onstott et al., 2014 and Lomstein et al., 2012), consistent with the idea that the amino acids within the bone are likely to be largely cellular (i.e. lipid-bound within living organisms) due to the discrepancy between DNA and amino acid stability over time.
claims.evidence: This is a calculation based on amino acid concentration data.

claims.claim: The amino acids within the bone are likely to be largely cellular due to the discrepancy between DNA and amino acid stability over time.
claims.source: This is fairly similar to the observed THAA concentration indicating ~3×108 cells/g (calculation of cell abundance from total amino acids based on that of Onstott et al., 2014 and Lomstein et al., 2012), consistent with the idea that the amino acids within the bone are likely to be largely cellular (i.e. lipid-bound within living organisms) due to the discrepancy between DNA and amino acid stability over time.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparing DNA and amino acid concentrations.

claims.claim: The DNA concentration in the adjacent mudstone matrix indicates a cell concentration of ~5×10^6 cells/g.
claims.source: The DNA concentration in the adjacent mudstone matrix indicate a cell concentration of ~5×106 cells/g, but the observed THAA concentration is consistent with a cell concentration of ~2×109 cells/g.
claims.evidence: This is a calculation based on DNA concentration data.

claims.claim: The subterranean dinosaur bone was enriched in cell-bound DNA relative to the mudstone matrix.
claims.source: These results suggest that the subterranean dinosaur bone was enriched in cell-bound DNA relative to the mudstone matrix.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the DNA concentration data.

claims.claim: EDTA-extracted structures appeared to contain DNA from cells that aggregate within these structures, consistent with a modern biofilm.
claims.source: Furthermore, EDTA-extracted structures appeared to contain DNA from cells that aggregate within these structures, consistent with a modern biofilm; the DNA itself had possibly been exposed due to the EDTA treatment.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the fluorescence microscopy results.

claims.claim: 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing revealed the predominance of Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria in subterranean Centrosaurus bone.
claims.source: The 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing revealed the predominance of Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria in subterranean Centrosaurus bone.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing.

claims.claim: Sequences affiliated with classes Nitriliruptoria and Deltaproteobacteria were more abundant in bone relative to adjacent mudstone or the surface scrapings from the bone itself.
claims.source: Sequences affiliated with classes Nitriliruptoria and Deltaproteobacteria were more abundant relative to adjacent mudstone or even the surface scrapings from the bone itself (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, with reference to Figure 9.

claims.claim: The majority of the sequences within Deltaproteobacteria were identified as belonging to the family Desulfurellaceae.
claims.source: The majority of the sequences within Deltaproteobacteria were identified as belonging to the family Desulfurellaceae, which contains some sulfur-respiring species.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing.

claims.claim: In Centrosaurus bone, about 30% of sequences were phylogenetically close to the genus Euzebya.
claims.source: In Centrosaurus bone, about 30% of sequences were phylogenetically close to the genus Euzebya, a deeply branching, aerobic, marine Actinobacterium (Appendix 1—figure 58).

claims.claim: Evidence is required to identify the type of protein, demonstrate its endogenous origin, and demonstrate its age.
claims.source: In addition to reliable markers of general protein presence (e.g. amide, succinimide, or piperazine pyrolysis products), evidence is required to identify the type of protein (i.e. amino acid composition or sequence) as well demonstrate its endogenous origin (e.g. localization) and age (i.e. degree of degradation as revealed by amino acid racemization, post-translational modifications such as deamidation, or peptide length/degree of hydrolysis).

claims.claim: Degradation of collagen polypeptides follows a pattern of gradual hydrolysis at the terminal ends followed by catastrophic degradation and rapid hydrolysis due to rupture of the triple helix quaternary structure.
claims.source: Degradation of collagen polypeptides follows a pattern of gradual hydrolysis of amino acids at the terminal ends followed by catastrophic degradation and rapid hydrolysis due to rupture of the triple helix quaternary structure, making the resulting gelatinous fragments susceptible to rapid leaching from the bone or microbial degradation (Collins et al., 1995; Collins et al., 2009; Dobberstein et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on collagen degradation.

claims.claim: If ancient collagen does persist in a fossil bone, then such preservation would often provide clear, strong structural and chemical signatures like that in the Pleistocene-Holocene shark teeth.

claims.source: However, our results here suggest that techniques like Py-GC-MS or HPLC that give more general information on protein presence versus absence or general amino acid composition should be considered frontline approaches when dealing with samples of significant age and/or thermal maturity (e.g. Demarchi et al., 2016; Hendy et al., 2018; Cappellini et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Treating Mesozoic bone that has experienced diagenesis, low latitudes, and permineralisation identically to more recent, less altered bone is ill-advised.
claims.source: Treating Mesozoic bone that has experienced diagenesis, low latitudes, and permineralisation identically to more recent, less altered bone is ill-advised, and any work on such samples should employ these fundamental methods before attempting to sequence peptides that might not be present, ancient, or endogenous.

results.result: Demineralization products of Cretaceous dinosaur bone differ structurally and chemically from modern and Pleistocene-Holocene controls. Dinosaur bone vessels are Si-dominated and inorganic, consistent with mineralized biofilms, while younger samples yield organic, collagen-rich fibrous masses.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C74 provide converging microscopy and EDS evidence showing that dinosaur bone demineralization products are structurally distinct (vessels vs. fibrous masses) and chemically distinct (Si-dominated vs. C/N/S-enriched) from controls. The interpretation that these structures represent mineralized biofilms is supported by elemental composition data and cited literature on biofilm mineralization.

results.result: ATR FTIR analysis detected organic peaks in dinosaur bone demineralization products that could be consistent with various organic bonds, but these are not necessarily ancient, endogenous, or protein-derived.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 appropriately present ATR FTIR data with cautious interpretation. The authors correctly note that detected bonds (CH, CO, amide) are simple and non-specific, and explicitly state limitations. This conservative interpretation is scientifically sound given the data quality and chemical ambiguity.

results.result: Py-GC-MS analysis shows dinosaur bone lacks clear protein pyrolysis products and instead resembles environmental sources (mudstone, humic acids). Weak evidence for kerogen-like n-alkane/n-alkene doublets was detected.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C85 present Py-GC-MS data showing dinosaur bone pyrograms differ from modern collagen-containing bone and resemble environmental controls. The interpretation is supported by comparative chromatograms (Figure 3). The cautious identification of weak kerogen signatures (C82, C85) is appropriate given data quality, though the authors acknowledge these require further validation.

results.result: Amino acid analysis reveals that subterranean dinosaur bone has a THAA profile dominated by Gly and Tyr that does not match collagen, with lower concentrations than modern bone. Surface exposure changes the amino acid profile toward that of surface-eroded bone.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C92 present HPLC amino acid data with appropriate statistical visualization (Figure 6, PCA). The finding that dinosaur bone THAA profiles differ from collagen is well-supported by compositional data and PCA separation. The observation that exposure changes amino acid profiles is supported by comparative analysis of matrix-surrounded vs. uncovered samples, though sample size is limited.

results.result: Late Cretaceous bone shows L-amino acid dominance with low racemization, suggesting the amino acids are not particularly ancient.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 present amino acid racemization data (Table 1) showing L-dominance in dinosaur bone. The interpretation that low racemization indicates recent amino acids is scientifically sound, as racemization is time-dependent. This finding is consistent with the contamination hypothesis.

results.result: Subterranean dinosaur bone has a different amino acid composition than surrounding mudstone, and surface-eroded bone shows similarity to topsoil. Matrix-surrounded bone shows the most distinct THAA profile, with greatest variation in Gly and Tyr.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C100 present comparative amino acid data between bone, mudstone, and topsoil with PCA visualization (Figure 6F). The statistical separation of sample types in PC space supports the interpretation of distinct amino acid sources. The observation of compositional changes with surface exposure is consistent with microbial colonization.

results.result: Topsoil shows high amino acid concentration with moderate racemization (active biological cycling), mudstone shows low concentration with recent amino acids (low residence time), and fossil bones show intermediate patterns suggesting preferential amino acid localization with recent biological activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C105 integrate amino acid concentration and racemization data to infer biological processes. The interpretations are logical given the data patterns: high concentration + racemization = active cycling; low concentration + L-dominance = low residence; intermediate = preferential accumulation. These inferences are consistent with microbial ecology principles.

results.result: Pleistocene-Holocene shark teeth contain THAA profiles matching collagen with high racemization, consistent with ancient, endogenous collagen preservation.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 present amino acid data from control samples showing collagen-like composition (Figure 6) and high racemization (Table 1). This provides a positive control demonstrating that the methods can detect ancient collagen when present, strengthening the negative findings for dinosaur bone.

results.result: Radiocarbon analysis shows dinosaur bone has TOC content similar to topsoil but lower than collagen-rich bone. The bone is not radiocarbon-dead but shows lower F14C than mudstone/topsoil, suggesting some ancient carbon mixed with recent environmental carbon (~26% from mudstone based on mixing model).
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C114 present radiocarbon data (Table 2) with quantitative mixing model calculation. The finding of non-radiocarbon-dead carbon in 66 Ma bone strongly supports contamination. The mixing model (C112) provides a quantitative estimate, though it relies on the assumption that all endogenous C is radiocarbon-dead, which is reasonable but should be stated as an assumption.

results.result: DNA concentration is ~50× higher in dinosaur bone than mudstone, indicating ~4×10^8 cells/g. PI staining reveals DNA in vessel-like structures. DNA and amino acid concentrations yield consistent cell abundance estimates, suggesting amino acids are largely cellular.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C123 present DNA quantification (Table 3) and fluorescence microscopy (Figure 8) with cell abundance calculations. The consistency between DNA-based and amino acid-based cell estimates (C117-C118) strengthens the interpretation. The observation of DNA in demineralized structures (C116, C123) supports biofilm interpretation, though the authors appropriately note EDTA may cause cell rupture.

results.result: 16S rRNA sequencing reveals dinosaur bone contains a distinct microbial community dominated by Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria, with enrichment of Nitriliruptoria and Deltaproteobacteria relative to mudstone. Statistical analysis (PCA, PERMANOVA) confirms significant differences between bone interior and surrounding matrix.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C131 present 16S rRNA sequencing data with appropriate statistical analysis. The PERMANOVA result (C129: F=53.16, p=0.0084) provides strong statistical support for community differences. PCA visualization (C128) and taxonomic composition data (Figure 9) converge to support the conclusion of a distinct bone microbiome. The identification of specific taxa (C126-C127) is appropriately cautious given short read limitations.

results.result: The Si-dominated composition and occasional infilling of dinosaur bone vessels is consistent with silicified biofilms. HCl demineralization may preferentially retrieve mineralized biofilms over organic material, and mineral infilling likely includes silicates with possible barite/gypsum.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C140 present interpretations of EDS and demineralization results. While the Si-dominance is well-documented (C67-C68), the interpretations involve multiple speculative elements: biofilm growth patterns (C132), differential preservation during demineralization (C134-C135), and mineral composition (C136). The authors appropriately acknowledge uncertainty (C138-C139) and recommend comparative studies (C140), but these interpretations require additional validation.

results.result: Early-eluting Py-GC-MS peaks in dinosaur bone may derive from humic acids or other non-protein sources. Weak kerogen signatures detected may represent intra-bone variation or could derive from soil contaminants rather than endogenous lipids.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C142, C150-C151 appropriately interpret Py-GC-MS data by considering alternative sources for detected compounds. The comparison to humic acid standards (C141, C150) and acknowledgment of potential soil contamination (C151) demonstrates scientific rigor. The cautious interpretation of weak kerogen signals (C143-C144) is appropriate given data quality.

results.result: Kerogen formation from endogenous lipids might not preserve tubular structures with high fidelity due to loss of amphipathic properties during hydrolysis. However, observed mineralization is more consistent with biofilm origin than kerogen origin.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C149 present theoretical considerations about kerogen formation with appropriate citation (C145: Rand and Parsegian, 1989). The logic that hydrolysis would disrupt membrane structure is sound. The conclusion that mineralization favors biofilm interpretation (C149) is supported by EDS data (C148) and cited biofilm literature.

results.result: L-amino acid dominance in dinosaur bone suggests recent input and endogenous degradation. Reversed Glx/Asx D/L ratios indicate bacterial contamination, consistent with peptidoglycans from gram-positive Actinobacteria cell walls.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C155 integrate amino acid racemization data with 16S rRNA sequencing results. The interpretation of reversed D/L ratios as bacterial contamination (C154) is supported by cited literature on peptidoglycan composition. The link to observed Actinobacteria dominance (C155) provides independent corroboration, though the quantitative cell wall composition estimate requires the cited reference to be accurate.

results.result: Differences in THAA composition between subterranean and surface-eroded bone suggest different microenvironments and microbial communities. Surface-eroded bone resembles topsoil communities. Brief aerial exposure may rapidly alter subterranean microbial communities. Bone may provide nutrient sources encouraging microbial proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C161 present interpretations of amino acid compositional differences with ecological reasoning. The observations are well-supported by data (Figures 6-7), though sample sizes are limited (acknowledged in C159). The interpretation of rapid contamination upon exposure (C160) is surprising but supported by comparative data between matrix-surrounded and uncovered samples. These inferences are consistent with microbial ecology principles.

results.result: Lower F14C in dinosaur bone compared to mudstone/topsoil suggests some biologically inaccessible, possibly ancient carbon. Potential sources include endogenous kerogen, mineralized biofilm carbon, or carbon trapped by biofilm formation faster than it exits.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C165 present speculative interpretations of radiocarbon data. While the observation of intermediate F14C is well-documented (C111), the proposed mechanisms (C163-C165) are speculative and not directly tested. The kerogen hypothesis (C163) is weakly supported by Py-GC-MS, and the biofilm mineralization hypothesis (C164) lacks direct evidence. These remain plausible hypotheses requiring further investigation.

results.result: EDTA-demineralized bone shows similar microbial community to non-demineralized bone, indicating that demineralized samples used in other taphonomic studies are amenable to nucleic acid analysis. PI staining likely results from EDTA-induced cell rupture.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C168 present practical methodological findings. The similarity of microbial communities (C166) is supported by 16S rRNA data and has important implications for studying 'soft tissues' (C167). The interpretation of PI staining (C168) is reasonable given EDTA's known effects on cell membranes.

results.result: The dominance of aerobic Euzebya is consistent with shallow burial depth, while Deltaproteobacteria presence suggests anaerobic niches within bone. The Actinobacteria dominance resembles findings from Neanderthal bone. Cell concentrations (~5×10^8 cells/g) indicate a substantial microbial community.
results.evaluation: Claims C169-C172 present ecological interpretations of 16S rRNA data. The reasoning about aerobic/anaerobic niches (C169-C170) is logical given burial depth and microbial physiology. The comparison to Neanderthal bone (C171) provides useful context with appropriate citation. Cell abundance estimates (C172) are supported by consistent DNA and amino acid calculations.

results.result: Dinosaur bone demineralization products differ structurally and elementally from Pleistocene-Holocene and modern controls. Younger samples yield collagen-rich organic masses, while shark teeth show taphonomic mineral accumulation (Fe, S) possibly from pyrite and/or N-heterocyclic polymers.
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C178 summarize and interpret microscopy/EDS findings with appropriate caution. The structural and elemental differences are well-documented. The interpretation of shark tooth Fe/S content (C175-C176) considers multiple possibilities. The discussion of N-heterocyclic polymers (C177-C178) appropriately cites relevant literature while noting that detected polymers could be exogenous.

results.result: FTIR peaks similar to those in dinosaur bone have been used as evidence for collagen in other studies, but such results are not conclusive. Amide bonds are not specific to peptides, and without peak deconvolution, organic bonds alone cannot identify collagen. Phosphate peak symmetry might indicate lower collagen content.
results.evaluation: Claims C179-C184 provide critical evaluation of FTIR methodology with appropriate citations. The authors correctly note limitations of using simple bond detection as evidence for ancient proteins (C180-C182). The discussion of phosphate peak interpretation (C183-C184) is appropriately cautious, noting methodological differences that may affect comparability. This represents sound scientific criticism of prior work.

results.result: Amino acids in dinosaur bone are dominated by non-collagen proteins and appear relatively recent. Low amino acid and D-amino acid concentrations, plus non-collagen THAA profiles, suggest most endogenous collagen has been lost. Taphonomic alteration would be expected at this age.
results.evaluation: Claims C185-C188 synthesize amino acid analysis results into coherent conclusions. The interpretation that endogenous collagen has been lost (C187) is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence: low concentration, low racemization, non-collagen composition. The acknowledgment of expected taphonomic alteration (C188) demonstrates appropriate consideration of preservation processes.

results.result: Pleistocene-Holocene shark teeth show high amino acid concentrations with collagen-like THAA profiles and high racemization. Ethanol rinsing did not change composition, suggesting insoluble collagen with preserved higher-order structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C189-C191 present control sample results demonstrating successful detection of ancient collagen. The ethanol rinsing experiment (C190) provides evidence for structural preservation rather than mobile peptides. High racemization (C191) confirms antiquity. These positive controls strengthen the negative findings for dinosaur bone by demonstrating method sensitivity.

results.result: Previous studies reporting dinosaur 'soft tissues' often do not fully address that fossil bones are biologically active open systems. Field observations show surface colonization by lichens and subsurface penetration by roots. Even deeply buried bone can be biologically active given subsurface microbial abundance. It is necessary to rule out contamination before concluding endogenous organic preservation.
results.evaluation: Claims C192-C198 provide critical context and recommendations. Field observations (C193) support the open system concept. Citations to deep biosphere research (C196, C220) provide strong support for subsurface biological activity. The recommendation to rule out contamination (C198) is scientifically sound. The note about fungal collagen production (C195) highlights an important but often overlooked contamination source.

results.result: No evidence of endogenous proteins was detected in the dinosaur bone studied, failing to replicate claims of Mesozoic protein survival. In contrast, Pleistocene-Holocene material shows clear evidence for ancient collagen. Claims of ancient proteins require corroborating evidence including protein identification, demonstration of endogenous origin, and evidence of age.
results.evaluation: Claims C199-C202 present the study's primary negative finding with appropriate context. The failure to detect endogenous proteins is supported by multiple analytical approaches. The contrast with positive controls (C200) strengthens the conclusion. The recommendations for evidence standards (C201-C202) are scientifically rigorous and appropriate for extraordinary claims.

results.result: Collagen degradation follows a pattern of gradual terminal hydrolysis followed by catastrophic degradation. If ancient collagen persists, it should show clear signatures like those in Pleistocene-Holocene teeth. Techniques like Py-GC-MS and HPLC should be frontline approaches for old/thermally mature samples before attempting peptide sequencing.
results.evaluation: Claims C203-C207 present methodological recommendations based on study findings. The description of collagen degradation (C203) is supported by cited literature. The recommendation for screening methods (C206-C207) is scientifically sound—attempting peptide sequencing without first confirming protein presence is inefficient and may yield false positives. This represents an important methodological contribution.

results.result: Fossil bone contains high concentrations of recent organics and likely provides an ideal microbial habitat. The absence of endogenous protein evidence and presence of diverse microbial communities urge caution regarding dinosaur 'soft tissue' claims. Results support the hypothesis that some demineralized fossil bone structures represent biofilms. Endogenous organics may be subject to microbial recycling unless in inaccessible forms.
results.evaluation: Claims C208-C216 synthesize study findings into major conclusions. The characterization of bone as a microbial habitat (C208-C209) is supported by DNA, amino acid, and 16S rRNA data. The biofilm hypothesis (C214) is supported by structural, chemical, and biological evidence. The recommendation to consider microbial presence throughout taphonomic history (C216) is scientifically sound and has important implications for paleontology.

results.result: Microbial communities interact with fossils throughout taphonomic history: immediately after death, during burial, and during uplift/erosion. Given that microbes inhabit the crust kilometers deep, bone likely remains biologically active even when buried hundreds of meters for millions of years. This makes verifying Mesozoic protein claims extremely challenging.
results.evaluation: Claims C217-C221 present a comprehensive taphonomic framework incorporating microbial processes. The temporal stages (C217, C219) are logical. Evidence for microbial protein utilization (C218) and deep biosphere activity (C220) is supported by citations. The conclusion about verification challenges (C221) follows logically from the extensive contamination potential demonstrated throughout the study.

results.result: The authors propose a null hypothesis that complex biomolecules from dinosaur bones represent recent contamination rather than original material, with testable predictions about compositional differences, microbial presence, and signatures of recent biological activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 present the study's conceptual framework. The null hypothesis (C53) is scientifically appropriate given theoretical and empirical considerations about protein stability. The testable predictions (C54-C56) are clearly stated and guide the analytical approach. This represents sound hypothesis-driven research design, and the subsequent results support the predictions.

results.result: Samples were collected from the Dinosaur Park Formation (Late Campanian) in Alberta, Canada, from a Centrosaurus apertus bonebed. Aseptic techniques were implemented during excavation, though truly sterile excavation is practically impossible in paleontological fieldwork.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C66 describe sample provenance and collection methodology. The geological and paleontological context is well-documented with appropriate citations (C59). The description of aseptic techniques (C65) and acknowledgment of limitations (C66) demonstrates methodological transparency. The authors appropriately qualify their use of 'aseptic' given practical constraints of field paleontology.

results.result: Historical context: Fossils were thought to lack original organics, but some molecules can survive. Dinosaur bone has been proposed to preserve collagen and soft tissues, but proteins/lipids are unstable and bone is an open system. Alternative interpretations suggest 'soft tissues' are biofilms.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 provide background context with appropriate citations. These establish the scientific controversy and competing hypotheses that motivate the study. The characterization of bone as an open system (C5) and mention of biofilm reinterpretations (C6) set up the study's approach.

results.result: Literature review: Ancient biomolecules including DNA, peptides, sterols, melanin, amino acids, and porphyrins have been found in fossils. Persistence times vary by molecule type and conditions: DNA ≤1 Ma, collagen longer but unclear, pigments hundreds of millions of years.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C24 summarize prior work on ancient biomolecules with appropriate citations. This provides context for understanding which molecules might reasonably persist and establishes the exceptional nature of claimed Mesozoic protein preservation. The cited age limits are from peer-reviewed sources.

results.result: Literature review: Dinosaur bone has been reported to contain DNA, collagen, and cellular structures, with collagen being a common target due to its stability. However, these reports have been criticized as contamination, statistical artifacts, or alternative materials (biofilms, minerals).
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C34 review prior claims and criticisms with extensive citations. This establishes the scientific controversy and justifies the need for the current study. The authors fairly present both claims of preservation and critical alternative interpretations.

results.result: Theoretical considerations: It remains unclear how organics would persist for tens of millions of years. Peptide bond half-lives are too short for Mesozoic preservation under standard conditions. Reported dinosaur peptides are >10× older than the oldest uncontested proteins. On theoretical and empirical grounds, 66 Ma protein persistence seems exceptional.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C46 present theoretical arguments against long-term protein preservation with appropriate citations to protein chemistry and degradation kinetics. The comparison of claimed dinosaur protein ages to accepted ancient protein ages (C42-C44) provides important context. These theoretical considerations justify skepticism and motivate empirical testing.

results.result: Literature review: Protein loss and contamination increase over time in ancient bone. Fossil bones are open systems with organic/microbial flux. A substantial deep biosphere of microorganisms exists, even in million-year-old permafrost, making fossil bone microbiome presence highly likely.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 review evidence for contamination potential with appropriate citations to deep biosphere research. This establishes the plausibility of microbial colonization of fossil bone and provides theoretical foundation for the contamination hypothesis. The citations to deep biosphere studies are from high-quality sources.
